title: Chapter 28.  Migration, Displacement & Rehabilitation — Beyond the Kashmiri Pandits

blocks.content: Chapter 19 introduced the Kashmiri Pandit displacement as the single most significant demographic event in J&K's recent social history. This chapter widens the lens to cover other displaced/migrant communities whose status is also periodically tested, particularly the West Pakistan Refugees and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) displaced persons.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Displacement issues in Jammu & Kashmir extend beyond Kashmiri Pandits to encompass West Pakistan Refugees (WPRs).
PoJK (Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir) Displaced Persons constitute a major segment of historical displacement in J&K.
Rehabilitation policies target multi-dimensional relief and resettlement for non-Kashmiri Pandit displaced populations.
Understanding the historical timelines and legal distinctions between various displaced communities is essential for competitive exams.

blocks.content: West Pakistan Refugees (WPRs) are families who migrated to the Jammu region (mostly settling around Jammu city and R S Pura) from what became West Pakistan at the time of Partition in 1947 — distinct from Kashmiri Pandits (who were displaced from within the Kashmir Valley itself, decades later, in 1990).

Under the OLD state-era Permanent Resident framework (Article 35A, Chapter 10), WPR families — despite having lived in J&K for generations since 1947 — were NOT granted Permanent Resident status, since this status could only be conferred on those who were state subjects as of specific historical cut-off dates predating Partition, meaning WPRs could not vote in J&K state assembly elections, could not purchase land, and could not hold state-government jobs, despite being full Indian citizens with voting rights in Lok Sabha elections.
Migration, Displacement & Rehabilitation — Beyond the Kashmiri Pandits

This WPR anomaly was one of the most frequently cited real-world illustrations of Article 35A's practical restrictiveness, and was specifically and directly resolved by the 2019 reorganisation's replacement of the Permanent Resident framework with the broader 'domicile' category (Chapter 14), which extended full local rights (including Assembly voting rights and property/employment rights) to WPR families for the first time.

★ EXAM POINT: West Pakistan Refugees (WPR) — Partition-era migrants to Jammu who, despite being Indian citizens since 1947, could not vote in J&K's OWN state assembly elections or hold state government jobs under the old Permanent Resident/Article 35A framework — this specific anomaly, and its resolution by the 2019 domicile reform, is a frequently tested real-world case illustrating both the old and new status frameworks in practice.

rows: Migrated from West Pakistan during the 1947 partition and settled in Jammu & Kashmir.
Displaced from areas of Jammu & Kashmir under Pakistan's illegal occupation in 1947, 1965, and 1971.

blocks.content: A separate category of displaced persons consists of those (and their descendants) who fled to the Jammu region from areas that came under Pakistani control following the 1947-48 war (i.e., from what India refers to as Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, PoJK) — a distinct group from both the Kashmiri Pandits and the WPRs, with its own specific rehabilitation and representation history.

As noted in Chapter 16, one of the 5 LG-nominated seats in the post-2019 J&K Assembly is specifically reserved to represent this PoJK-displaced community, alongside separate nominated representation for Kashmiri migrants (Pandits) — a structural, representational response to these two historically distinct displacement categories.

items: Differentiate between West Pakistan Refugees (WPRs) and PoJK Displaced Persons regarding domicile rights and voting eligibility.
Understand major government rehabilitation packages provided to PoJK displaced families.
Analyze post-2019 legal changes affecting refugee rights and property ownership in Jammu & Kashmir.

As detailed in Chapter 19, the Kashmiri Pandit exodus of 1990 remains the most socially and politically significant displacement event in J&K's recent history, with rehabilitation efforts including dedicated residential colonies for returning families, reserved government employment quotas, and financial relief/compensation schemes implemented with varying uptake and continuing debate over their adequacy.

The Prime Minister's Development Package (originally announced in 2015, with subsequent phases) included provisions specifically aimed at facilitating the return and rehabilitation of displaced Kashmiri Pandit families, including employment and housing components.

West Pakistan Refugees (WPRs): Partition-era migrants to Jammu region who, despite being Indian citizens, lacked J&K Permanent Resident status pre-2019 (no state-assembly vote, no land purchase, no state jobs).
2019 'domicile' reform (replacing 'Permanent Resident') extended full local rights to WPR families for the first time.
PoJK-displaced persons = a distinct category from both Kashmiri Pandits and WPRs; specifically represented via one of the 5 nominated Assembly seats.
Kashmiri Pandit rehabilitation includes the PM's Development Package (2015 onward) with housing/employment components for returning families.
